message.content:
First read /tmp/AGENT_GUIDE.md carefully (rules + engine API). You work in a git worktree of /workspace (build with `cargo build --release` in your worktree root).

YOUR TASK: find and fix discrepancies between our JS ENGINE and the ORIGINAL binary for core ECMAScript language semantics and the standard builtins. Files you own: `src/lexer.rs`, `src/parser.rs`, `src/ast.rs`, `src/resolver.rs`, `src/compiler.rs`, `src/bytecode.rs`, `src/vm.rs`, `src/props.rs`, `src/ops.rs`, `src/object.rs`, `src/value.rs`, `src/realm.rs`, `src/loader.rs`, `src/builtins/*.rs` EXCEPT `intl.rs`, `temporal.rs` (other agents own those). Do NOT edit `src/runtime/*` (other agents own them) — except you may fix `src/runtime/timers.rs`/`src/runtime/mod.rs` event-loop bugs if a core issue requires it (minimal, documented).

Method: write many small JS programs (in /tmp/coreagent/) exercising language features a test-writer would use — classes (fields, private methods/accessors, static blocks, accessors, super, new.target, inheritance from builtins), generators/async generators (return/throw, yield* delegation with return/throw, for-await with sync iterables), async/await microtask ORDERING vs the original (print interleavings), destructuring corner cases, default params scope, closures in loops, labeled statements, switch/case lexical scoping, try/catch/finally completion values, getters/setters, Proxy traps + invariants, Reflect, Symbol registry and well-knowns (toPrimitive, iterator, hasInstance, toStringTag, species, isConcatSpreadable, unscopables, match/replace/split), JSON edge cases, RegExp objects (lastIndex handling, sticky, named groups, replace callbacks, split limits; the regex engine itself in src/regexp/ is verified — read its doc comment), String/Array/Object/Number/Math/Date/Map/Set/WeakMap/WeakRef/typed arrays/ArrayBuffer/DataView/Atomics/BigInt methods, iterator helpers, Array.fromAsync, structured errors (messages of every TypeError/RangeError/ReferenceError/SyntaxError you can trigger — compare `e.message` with the original), eval/new Function/with/arguments object (mapped arguments in sloppy mode!), getter/setter on classes, tagged templates/raw strings, numeric separators, optional chaining with calls, exponent operator precedence, comma/void/typeof/delete semantics, sloppy vs strict mode differences, global object properties (var/function at top level of scripts), Function.prototype.toString outputs, property enumeration orders, sort stability/comparators, Object.prototype.toString tags, labeled continue, closures capturing per-iteration bindings, TDZ errors, const assignment errors, `this` binding rules, call-stack depth limit ("Maximum call stack size exceeded": the original's limit is 1500 frames incl. native frames; CJS main uses 5), stack trace strings (`err.stack`: frames are function names in `vm.trace`), SyntaxError messages for invalid programs (via eval and via files: the CLI prints `SyntaxError: <msg> (line N)` for -e/stdin scripts and `Uncaught SyntaxError: <msg>` for files).
Known issues to fix (reported by other agents):
 1. `for (const x of undefined){}` → original message ``cannot read property '\u00001' of undefined`` (NUL char then 1), ours "value is not iterable". (Same family: array destructuring of null/undefined already uses this text in vm.rs DestructIter.)
 2. Unhandled-rejection report order: `const P = Promise.reject(Error('P')); const Q = Promise.reject(Error('Q')); P.then(()=>{});` prints P then Q in the original, Q then P in ours (see runtime/mod.rs report_unhandled_rejections + builtins/promise.rs; you may fix in those).
 3. `new Uint8Array(3).set([1,2,3,4])` → original "source is too large for the target at offset"; negative offset → "TypedArray.prototype.set offset is negative".
 4. `import('./m.js')` from a CommonJS main script: original loads it relative to the script dir; ours fails (modules.rs dynamic_import uses frame.module which is None in CJS — use the calling script's directory; you may edit src/modules.rs).
Also look at performance hot spots if something is egregiously slow (e.g. a loop of 10M iterations, string concatenation in loops, property access) — compare timing with the original on simple benchmarks; the VM design is a stack bytecode interpreter in vm.rs (run_inner).

Iterate: find a difference, fix it, re-run all your tests (keep a regression suite in /tmp/coreagent/). Commit frequently in your worktree branch. Final reply: branch/commit, list of fixes, remaining known differences.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.

# Guide for subagents working on the lumen reimplementation

## The project
We are reimplementing, from scratch in Rust (std only, NO external crates), a JavaScript engine +
Node/Bun-like runtime called "lumen" (CLI `lumen-cli`). The ORIGINAL compiled binary is at
`/workspace/executable` (symlink `/tmp/orig`). Our reimplementation lives in the git repo `/workspace`
(you will be working in your own git worktree copy of it). Hidden tests will run JS programs through
both binaries and compare stdout, stderr and exit code EXACTLY, so fidelity to the original's
observable behavior (output formats, error messages, property orders, edge cases) is the goal.

## Rules (strict)
- You may RUN the original (`/tmp/orig file.js`, `/tmp/orig -e 'code'`) to observe behavior.
- You MUST NOT disassemble/decompile/read the original binary's bytes, use strace/ltrace/gdb on it,
  search the internet, or download anything. No network is available anyway.
- Do not copy JS source code text of the original's internal modules verbatim (some functions print
  their JS source via `String(fn)`; you may observe *behavior*, but write your own Rust implementation).
- Write Rust (std only). Keep any scratch scripts (shell/python/JS test files) OUTSIDE the repo, e.g.
  under `/tmp/<yourname>/`. Do not add non-Rust code files to the repo.
- Only edit the files assigned to you. If a core-engine bug blocks you, work around it in your files
  if possible and describe the bug precisely in your final report (file/function, repro JS). If you
  absolutely must touch a shared file, keep the change minimal and list it in your report.
- Never run `/workspace/compile.sh` and never write to `/workspace/executable`.
- Build with `cargo build --release` in YOUR worktree (binary: `target/release/lumen`). Commit your
  work in your worktree with clear messages when done (and at milestones).
- `console.log` in lumen prints values via `String(v)` (objects print as `[object Object]`), so when
  probing the original use JSON.stringify or explicit string building.

## Engine architecture (what you need to write builtins)
Key modules (in `src/`): `value.rs` (Value, JsStr, Sym, PropKey), `object.rs` (Obj, ObjKind, Prop,
PropDesc, Args, NativeFn, flags WRITABLE/ENUMERABLE/CONFIGURABLE, WEC, WC), `vm.rs` (Vm, JsResult,
calls, errors, frames, Job), `props.rs` (property internal methods on Vm), `ops.rs` (conversions),
`realm.rs` (intrinsics + helpers to define builtins), `builtins/*` (ECMAScript builtins),
`runtime/*` (node/web runtime), `runtime/mod.rs` (Host state, event loop), `modules.rs` (ESM).

### Values
```rust
enum Value { Undefined, Null, Bool(bool), Num(f64), Str(JsStr), Sym(Sym), BigInt(Rc<BigInt>), Obj(Obj), Empty /*internal*/ }
JsStr::from_str("x"), s.to_rust_string(), s.units() -> &[u16] (UTF-16), JsStr::from_units(vec), JsStr::concat(&a,&b)
Value::str("x"), Value::Num(1.0), v.is_undefined(), v.is_nullish(), v.as_obj() -> Option<&Obj>, v.truthy(), v.is_callable()
PropKey::from_str("name"), PropKey::Str(js), PropKey::Sym(sym), PropKey::from_index(i)
```
### Natives
```rust
type NativeFn = fn(&mut Vm, &Args) -> JsResult<Value>;   // JsResult<T> = Result<T, Value /*thrown*/>
// Args: a.this (Value), a.args (&[Value]), a.arg(i) -> Value (undefined if missing), a.callee (&Obj),
//       a.new_target (Option<Obj>, Some when called with `new`), a.slot(i) -> captured data (see native_closure)
vm.native_fn("name", length, f) -> Obj                         // function object
vm.native_closure("name", length, f, vec![slot0, slot1]) -> Obj // with captured Values (read via a.slot(i))
vm.def_method(&obj, "name", length, f) -> Obj                    // non-enumerable writable configurable method
vm.def_getter(&obj, "name", f); vm.def_accessor(&obj, "name", getter, setter)
vm.native_ctor("Name", length, f, &proto) -> Obj   // constructor; links proto.constructor & ctor.prototype
// In a constructor native: let p = vm.proto_from_nt(&a.new_target, &fallback_proto)?; Obj::new(Some(p), kind)
vm.make_ctor(&fobj)  // mark a native fn as constructible
vm.def_global("Name", Value::Obj(o)); vm.set_tag(&obj, "Tag") // Symbol.toStringTag
```
### Objects
```rust
vm.new_object() -> Obj (plain, Object.prototype); vm.obj_from(vec![("k", v), ...]) -> Obj (enumerable props)
vm.new_array(vec![...]) -> Obj; Obj::new(proto: Option<Obj>, ObjKind::Ordinary)
o.set_str("k", v, WEC); o.set_prop(PropKey, v, flags); o.get_own_str("k") -> Option<Value> (own data only)
o.borrow() / o.borrow_mut()  (RefCell — never hold a borrow across a call into JS!)
// custom native state: Obj::new(Some(proto), ObjKind::Host(Box::new(MyState{..}))) and later
//   if let ObjKind::Host(h) = &o.borrow().kind { if let Some(s) = h.downcast_ref::<MyState>() {..} }
//   (use Cell/RefCell inside MyState for mutation)
crate::runtime::reorder_enum(vm, &obj, &["a","b",...]) // force enumerable key order (missing -> noop fns)
```
### Property access / conversions (all on `vm`)
```rust
vm.get(&obj, &key, &receiver_value)?; vm.get_str(&obj, "name")?; vm.get_prop_of(&value, &key)? (works on primitives)
vm.set_prop_of(&value, key, v, /*strict*/ true)?; vm.create_data_property(&obj, key, v)?
vm.has_property(&obj, &key)?; vm.delete(&obj, &key)?; vm.own_property_keys(&obj)?; vm.enumerable_own_keys(&obj)?
vm.to_string(&v)? -> JsStr; vm.to_number(&v)?; vm.to_object(&v)?; vm.to_property_key(&v)?; vm.to_index(&v)?
vm.to_integer_or_infinity(&v)?; vm.to_int32/to_uint32; vm.to_primitive(&v, crate::ops::Hint::Default)?
crate::runtime::display_value(vm, &v) -> String   // what console.log prints for a value
crate::runtime::util::inspect_value(vm, &v, depth)? -> String  // util.inspect
```

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

# lumen

A from-scratch JavaScript **engine** in Rust — std only, zero dependencies — and a
**runtime** being built on top of it, the way Node/Deno/Bun wrap a JS engine with an event
loop and host APIs. Every crate in the workspace is std-only: no `tokio`, `mio`, `libc`,
`rustyline`, `serde`, or any other third-party dependency, anywhere.

## The engine (`crates/lumen`)

A lexer, parser, and **three execution tiers**:

- a **tree-walking interpreter** — the reference oracle: the spec semantics live here, and
  every other tier must match it observably (a differential fuzzer, `lumen-difftest`, holds
  them to that);
- an opt-in **bytecode VM** — functions compile whole (or not at all — no deoptimization) to
  a stack machine with slot-homed locals, per-site inline caches for property and free-name
  access backed by object shapes (hidden classes), and dense-array element fast paths;
- a **native template JIT** — bytecode lowers to real ARM64 machine code on macOS, Linux,
  and Windows, with a correctness-first x86-64 backend on Intel macOS, Linux, and Windows:
  per-op templates with the interpreter as the shared slow path, inline-cache reads baked
  into the instruction stream, fused compare-and-branch, exact-`ToInt32` bitops, and numeric
  *register chains* that keep runs of arithmetic entirely in FP registers. The full set of
  inline fast paths currently lives in the ARM64 backend; x86-64 starts with native control
  flow and checked per-op helpers. Other architectures degrade to the bytecode VM.

Tier selection: `--tier=interp|bytecode|jit` (**jit is the default**; where the JIT is
unavailable it degrades to the bytecode VM). Functions tier up after a call-count threshold —
immediately if the body contains a loop. Force the reference tree-walker with `--tier=interp`
(or `LUMEN_TIER=interp`).

The language surface: generators and `async`/`await` running on stackful coroutines (async
bodies suspend on the bytecode VM itself), full `RegExp` (including `\p{…}` and inline
modifiers), typed arrays, `Proxy`/`Reflect`, ES modules (top-level await, `import defer`,
source phase), `Intl`, and `Temporal`.

`Intl` (ECMA-402) and `Temporal` are behind the default-on `intl` and `temporal` Cargo features.
The CLDR data tables included by `intl` are the largest single contributor to binary size (~3 MB
of the release binary). Build with `--no-default-features` for a small engine: the `Intl` and
`Temporal` globals are absent, `Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant` is omitted, and the `toLocale*`
methods degrade to their locale-independent forms, the way engines built without i18n do. Either
feature can be enabled independently.

On dependencies and `unsafe`: the workspace stays std-only — the JIT maps executable memory
through raw platform declarations (`mmap`/`mprotect`, macOS `MAP_JIT`, or Windows
`VirtualAlloc`/`VirtualProtect`) rather than libc. Pages are writable only while code is copied,
then executable/read-only, and instruction caches are synchronized where required. The
interpreter and bytecode VM are safe Rust; `unsafe` is concentrated where machine
code meets the object graph (the JIT's executable pages and its templates' raw reads — every
baked offset is *measured at runtime* against the live types and fails closed to the checked
helper if anything doesn't hold) and in the N-API addon loader's `dlopen` bridge.

// Bytecode definitions shared by compiler and VM.

use crate::ast::FuncKind;
use crate::value::*;
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum BindKind {
    Var,
    Let,
    Const,
    Class,
    Function,
    Param,
    CatchParam,
    /// internal bindings: this, arguments, new.target, home, private names
    Internal,
    /// the name of a named function expression (immutable, silently ignores writes in sloppy)
    FuncName,
    Import,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ScopeInfo {
    pub names: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub kinds: Vec<BindKind>,
    pub is_function: bool,
}

impl ScopeInfo {
    pub fn find(&self, name: &JsStr) -> Option<usize> {
        self.names.iter().position(|n| n == name)
    }
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MethodTarget {
    Proto,
    Ctor,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MKind {
    Method,
    Getter,
    Setter,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct TemplateData {
    pub cooked: Vec<Option<JsStr>>,
    pub raw: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub id: usize,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
pub enum Op {
    // constants
    Undef,
    Null,
    True,
    False,
    Int(i32),
    Const(u32),
    Empty,
    // stack
    Pop,
    Dup,
    Dup2,
    Swap,
    /// [a b c] -> [c a b]
    Rot3,
    /// [a b c d] -> [d a b c]
    Rot4,
    /// copy the value n below the top: [.. x a1..an] -> [.. x a1..an x]
    Pick(u16),
    // locals / env
    GetLocal(u32),
    GetLocalChk(u32, u32),
    SetLocal(u32),
    InitLocal(u32),
    ClearLocal(u32),
    GetEnv(u16, u32),
    GetEnvChk(u16, u32, u32),
    SetEnv(u16, u32),
    SetEnvChk(u16, u32, u32),
    InitEnv(u16, u32),
    GetName(u32),
    SetName(u32),
    TypeofName(u32),
    DeleteName(u32),
    /// pushes [this, func] for a call to an identifier (with-scope aware)
    GetNameCall(u32),
    GetGlobal(u32),
    SetGlobal(u32),
    TypeofGlobal(u32),
    /// declare global var (name, is_function)
    DeclareGlobalVar(u32),
    DeclareGlobalFunc(u32),
    DeclareGlobalLex(u32, bool),
    InitGlobalLex(u32),
    PushScope(u32),
    PopScope,
    CopyScope,
    PushWith,
    ThrowConst(u32),
    // function frame
    This,
    ThisChk,
    SetThis,
    NewTarget,
    GetArg(u32),
    GetRest(u32),
    CreateArguments(bool),
    Callee,
    Home,
    // properties
    GetProp(u32),
    GetPropOpt(u32),
    GetElem,
    SetProp(u32),
    SetElem,
    DeleteProp(u32),
    DeleteElem,
    GetSuper(u32),
    GetSuperElem,
    SetSuper(u32),

    PrivateIn,

    BindThisEnv(u16, u32),

pub struct FunctionCode {
    pub name: JsStr,
    pub ops: Vec<Op>,
    pub consts: Vec<Value>,
    pub keys: Vec<PropKey>,
    pub funcs: Vec<Rc<FunctionCode>>,
    pub scopes: Vec<Rc<ScopeInfo>>,
    pub templates: Vec<Rc<TemplateData>>,
    pub regexps: Vec<(JsStr, JsStr)>,
    pub strings: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub nlocals: u32,
    pub length: u32,
    pub kind: FuncKind,
    pub is_async: bool,
    pub is_generator: bool,
    pub strict: bool,
    pub source: Rc<str>,
    pub src_start: usize,
    pub src_end: usize,
    pub is_arrow: bool,
    pub has_simple_params: bool,
    pub line: u32,
    /// a function with no own `prototype` (methods, arrows, async functions, ...)
    pub no_prototype: bool,
    pub class_source: bool,
    /// name set from a class/declaration (affects toString for default ctor)
    pub is_default_ctor: bool,
    pub is_script: bool,
    pub is_module: bool,
    pub is_eval: bool,
}

impl FunctionCode {
    pub fn is_constructor(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.kind, FuncKind::Normal | FuncKind::ClassConstructor | FuncKind::DerivedConstructor)
            && !self.is_async
            && !self.is_generator
    }
    pub fn source_text(&self) -> String {
        if self.is_default_ctor {
            return String::new();
        }
        self.source.chars().skip(self.src_start).take(self.src_end.saturating_sub(self.src_start)).collect()
    }
}

impl std::fmt::Debug for FunctionCode {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        writeln!(f, "function {} (locals={}, strict={})", self.name, self.nlocals, self.strict)?;
        for (i, op) in self.ops.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "  {:4} {:?}", i, op)?;
        }
        for (i, func) in self.funcs.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "-- nested #{}:", i)?;
            write!(f, "{:?}", func)?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

#!/bin/bash
# usage: diffall.sh file.js...  -- combined stdout+stderr diff per file (orig vs ours)
LUMEN=${LUMEN:-/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-ac59a005e41a4405b/target/release/lumen}
for f in "$@"; do
  d=$(dirname "$f"); b=$(basename "$f")
  ( cd "$d"; timeout 10 /tmp/orig "$b" > /tmp/coreagent/.d1 2>&1 )
  ( cd "$d"; timeout 10 $LUMEN "$b" > /tmp/coreagent/.d2 2>&1 )
  if ! cmp -s /tmp/coreagent/.d1 /tmp/coreagent/.d2; then
    echo "== $f"
    diff -a /tmp/coreagent/.d1 /tmp/coreagent/.d2 | head -${LINES_MAX:-60}
  fi
done

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

# Optimizing JIT work

The first implemented pass is backward local liveness over the existing target-neutral
control-flow graph (`jit_ir/liveness.rs`). ARM64 local-load lowering transfers ownership
at proven last uses, avoiding a clone and the original slot's eventual drop. The source
slot becomes `undefined`; the normal TDZ check still runs before the transfer. This
works for every value representation, including BigInt.

The analysis joins successor live sets and iterates to a fixed point across backedges.
Unknown instructions keep all slots live. Captured/aliased frames, exception handlers,
frames above 128 slots and chunks above 4096 instructions are excluded. Failure to
converge within the compile-time budget also declines the optimization. Other native
regions continue using their existing emitters; this pass does not replace their
register allocation or introduce speculative deoptimization.

Set `LUMEN_JIT_NO_LAST_USES=1` to disable the pass for comparison. `LUMEN_JIT_FAST`
continues to control local-load lowering through its existing bit 3.

## Initial evidence

On Apple M4, preliminary three-round comparisons with the same release executable,
alternating the pass on and off, were effectively flat:

| Workload | Disabled median | Enabled median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 5000 DeltaBlue iterations | 9802 ms | 9758 ms |
| 10000 Djot parse/render iterations | 6064 ms | 6047 ms |

These differences are within noise, and some runs overlapped development compilation; the shared machine also had unrelated
compiler activity.
They are not evidence of an application speedup. A quiet rerun is required before
making any performance claim. The pass is an initial reusable optimization, not the
completed milestone of improving both DeltaBlue and a real application substantially.

Five-second native sampling showed reference-counting, allocation and cycle collection
in both workloads. Djot additionally executes significant AST-interpreter work; its
hot-function log includes arrows reading lexical `this`, class constructors and renderer
methods. Sampling does not by itself establish how much any proposed change will save.

The next work needs to address those costs: broaden compilation coverage for real
application functions, then use shared IR facts for register-resident values and guarded
inlining across operations. Heap work should be guided by measured collector/allocation
costs. Keep the interpreter as the semantic oracle throughout.

## Reproducing the parser workload

From the repository root:

```sh
(cd examples/djot-parser && npm ci --ignore-scripts)
bun build examples/djot-parser/bench.mjs --target=browser --format=iife --outfile=/tmp/lumen-djot.js
cargo build --release -p lumen --bin lumen
LUMEN_JIT_NO_LAST_USES=1 target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
node /tmp/lumen-djot.js
bun /tmp/lumen-djot.js
```

The bundle isolates engine execution from module-loader differences. Bun is only a
benchmark build tool. Every iteration verifies the complete rendered HTML against the
reference output. The timer includes tier warmup but excludes initial bundle loading.
Run engines sequentially, alternate ordering and compare several fresh processes.

    x = a[i] if i < len(a) else ''
    y = b[i] if i < len(b) else ''
    if x != y:
        pairs[(x, y)] += 1
        examples.setdefault((x, y), s[:160])
for (x, y), c in pairs.most_common():
    print(c, '| ORIG:', x, '| OURS:', y)
    print('    ', examples[(x, y)])

import sys
# usage: synpairs.py file.js out1 out2 -- print source + both messages for differing lines (1 output line per u() call)
src = [l for l in open(sys.argv[1]).read().split('\n') if l.startswith('u(')]
a = open(sys.argv[2]).read().split('\n')
b = open(sys.argv[3]).read().split('\n')
from collections import Counter
pairs = Counter()
examples = {}
for i, s in enumerate(src):
    x = a[i] if i < len(a) else ''
    y = b[i] if i < len(b) else ''
    if x != y:
        pairs[(x, y)] += 1
        examples.setdefault((x, y), s[:160])
for (x, y), c in pairs.most_common():
    print(c, '| ORIG:', x, '| OURS:', y)
    print('    ', examples[(x, y)])

import random, sys, re, json, glob
seed = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 1
n = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 300
random.seed(seed)
snippets = [
 'function f(a, b = 1, ...c) { return a + b; }', 'class A extends B { #x = 1; static y; constructor() { super(); } get z() { return this.#x; } }',
 'for (let i = 0; false; i++) { if (i % 2) continue; }', 'const { a, b: [c, d = 2], ...e } = obj;', 'async function g() { await x; for await (const y of z) {} }',
 'function* h() { yield 1; yield* other(); }', 'label: while (false) { break label; }', 'try { throw new Error("x"); } catch ({ message }) { } finally { }',
 'switch (x) { case 1: y(); break; default: z(); }', 'const f = async (a, { b }) => { return a ?? b; };', 'x = a ? b : c, d = e?.f?.[g]?.(h);',
 'let s = `a${b}c${`d${e}`}`;', 'obj = { a, b: 1, [c]: 2, get d() { return 3; }, set d(v) {}, async *e() {}, ...f };', 'arr = [1, , 3, ...rest];',
 'if (a) b(); else if (c) d(); else { e(); }', 'do { x++; } while (x < 5);', 'var re = /ab+c/gi, n = 0x1F + 1e3 + 1_000n;', 'new Foo(...args).bar`tpl`;',
 'import("mod").then(m => m.default);', 'delete obj[key]; void 0; typeof x === "undefined";', 'a ||= b; c &&= d; e ??= f; g **= 2;',
 'class C { static { init(); } accessor q = 1; }', 'with (obj) { prop; }', '(function () { "use strict"; return this; })();',
 'for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(o)) console.log(k, v);', 'for (var p in o) if (Object.hasOwn(o, p)) n++;', 'x => x * 2; (a, b) => ({ a, b });',
]
tokre = re.compile(r'\s+|`[^`]*`|"[^"]*"|/[^/\n]+/[gimsuy]*|\d[\w.]*|[A-Za-z_$#][\w$]*|\.\.\.|\?\?=|\?\.|\*\*=|&&=|\|\|=|=>|===|!==|==|!=|<=|>=|\+\+|--|&&|\|\||\?\?|\*\*|[{}()\[\];,.:?+\-*/%=<>!&|^~@]')
inserts = ['(', ')', '{', '}', '[', ']', ';', ',', '=', '=>', 'let', 'const', 'yield', 'await', 'async', 'function', 'class', 'new', 'super', 'this', '...', '?.', '.', 'return', 'break', 'continue', 'import', 'export', '#p', '@', '`', '"', '/', '1', 'a', 'static', 'get', 'set', 'in', 'of', '++', 'delete', 'typeof', 'enum', 'eval', 'arguments', 'default', 'case']
def tokens(s):
    return [m.group(0) for m in tokre.finditer(s)]
out = []
print('function u(src) { try { new Function(src); console.log("OK") } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name + ": " + e.message) } }')
for i in range(n):
    s = random.choice(snippets)
    toks = tokens(s)
    nonws = [j for j, t in enumerate(toks) if not t.isspace()]
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 2)):
        r = random.random()
        j = random.choice(nonws)
        if r < 0.35:
            toks[j] = ''
        elif r < 0.65:
            toks.insert(j, ' ' + random.choice(inserts) + ' ')
        elif r < 0.8:
            k = random.choice(nonws)
            toks[j], toks[k] = toks[k], toks[j]
        else:
            toks[j] = toks[j] + ' ' + toks[j]
        nonws = [j for j, t in enumerate(toks) if t and not t.isspace()]
        if not nonws:
            break
    src = ''.join(toks)
    print('u(%s); // %d' % (json.dumps(src), i))

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms
